title: Circulatory System

toc.title: 7.1 The heart, the heartbeat, the cardiac cycle and cardiac output
7.2 Arterial and venous systems; blood pressure

html:
The circulatory system carries 3 of the 40 Zoology questions — the largest share of the human physiology units. The paper draws on four blocks: the heart (chambers, valves, conducting system, cardiac cycle and output), the vessels and blood pressure, the blood (cells, clotting, ABO and Rh groups), and the disorders (atherosclerosis, heart attack, angina, varicose veins, anaemia). Almost every question is a name, a number or a direction of flow. The three traps that decide marks are: the left ventricle has the thickest wall, the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood, and O negative is the universal donor for red cells.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Anatomy: four chambers, the tricuspid and bicuspid (mitral) valves, the two semilunar valves, and the great vessels; the left ventricle wall is the thickest because it drives the systemic circuit.
  • Double circulation: right heart → lungs → left heart (pulmonary); left heart → body → right heart (systemic); the coronary arteries come from the ascending aorta.
  • Conducting system: SA node → AV node → bundle of His → right and left branches → Purkinje fibres; the SA node is the pacemaker because it depolarises fastest.
  • Cardiac cycle (0.8 s at 72/min): atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, diastole 0.5 s; S1 = AV valves closing, S2 = semilunar valves closing.
  • Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate ≈ 70 mL × 72 ≈ 5 L min⁻¹; ejection fraction ≈ 60 %.
  • ECG: P = atrial depolarisation, QRS = ventricular depolarisation, T = ventricular repolarisation.
  • Vessels: arteries thick-walled, no valves, high pressure; veins thin-walled, valves, low pressure; the hepatic portal vein runs gut → liver.
  • Blood pressure 120/80; hypertension ≥ 140/90; baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch.
  • Blood: plasma 55 %, cells 45 %; RBC 5 million/mm³, 120 days; WBC 4000–11 000/mm³; platelets 1.5–4 lakh/mm³; ABO and Rh groups; O− donor, AB+ recipient; erythroblastosis fetalis.

7.1 The heart, the heartbeat, the cardiac cycle and cardiac output

Position and coverings

The heart is a hollow muscular organ of about 250–300 g, roughly the size of the owner's fist, lying in the mediastinum between the lungs, behind the sternum. Two-thirds of it lies to the left of the midline, and its apex points down and to the left, reaching the fifth intercostal space about 9 cm from the midline.

It is enclosed in the pericardium: a tough outer fibrous layer and a serous layer of two sheets — the parietal lining the sac and the visceral stuck to the heart (the epicardium). Between them is a film of pericardial fluid that lets the heart move without friction.

The wall has three layers:

Layer Structure Note
Epicardium visceral serous pericardium + fat carries the coronary vessels
Myocardium cardiac muscle thickest in the left ventricle
Endocardium endothelium + connective tissue lines the chambers and valves

The chambers and valves

Chamber Receives Sends blood to Wall
Right atrium superior and inferior vena cava, coronary sinus right ventricle thin
Right ventricle right atrium pulmonary artery moderate
Left atrium four pulmonary veins left ventricle thin
Left ventricle left atrium aorta thickest

The two atria are separated by the interatrial septum, which bears the fossa ovalis — the remnant of the fetal opening. The ventricles are separated by the thick interventricular septum.

There are four valves, all of which open and close passively with the pressure difference across them:

Valve Position Opens when Prevents
Tricuspid (right AV) between right atrium and ventricle atrial pressure > ventricular backflow into the right atrium
Bicuspid / mitral (left AV) between left atrium and ventricle atrial pressure > ventricular backflow into the left atrium
Pulmonary semilunar at the exit of the right ventricle ventricular pressure > pulmonary artery backflow into the right ventricle
Aortic semilunar at the exit of the left ventricle ventricular pressure > aorta backflow into the left ventricle

The AV valves are held by chordae tendineae attached to papillary muscles, which stop them turning inside out during ventricular contraction.

Why the left ventricle is thickest

It pumps blood round the whole body, so it must generate about 120 mmHg; the right ventricle only pumps to the lungs, at about 25 mmHg. A question that offers "the right ventricle, because it is larger" is testing this.

The double circulation and the coronary circulation

Blood passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit:

  • Pulmonary circulation: right ventricle → pulmonary trunk → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium. Short, low pressure.
  • Systemic circulation: left ventricle → aorta → all the tissues → superior and inferior vena cava → right atrium. Long, high pressure.

This is why the heart is described as a double pump and why the two sides never mix in a healthy adult.

The heart muscle itself is fed by the coronary circulation. The right and left coronary arteries arise from the ascending aorta just above the aortic valve, and their branches run in the epicardium. Blood returns by the cardiac veins into the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium. The coronary arteries fill mainly during diastole, when the ventricle is relaxed — one reason a very fast heart rate is dangerous.

The conducting system

Cardiac muscle contracts without any nerve: it is myogenic. A special patch of muscle, the sinoatrial (SA) node, in the wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava, depolarises spontaneously about 70–80 times a minute and sets the rhythm. The wave then travels:

SA node → atria → AV node → bundle of His → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres → ventricular muscle.

Part Rate if it acts alone (per min) Conduction velocity
SA node 70–80 (the pacemaker) slow
AV node 40–60 0.05 m s⁻¹ — the slowest, giving a 0.1 s delay
Bundle of His and branches 30–40 1–2 m s⁻¹
Purkinje fibres 20–40 4 m s⁻¹ — the fastest

The SA node sets the rhythm because its membrane leaks ions so that it reaches threshold first; it therefore drives the other, slower pacemakers before they can fire on their own. They are latent pacemakers, ready to take over if the SA node fails.

The AV nodal delay matters: it lets the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract, so the ventricles are properly filled.

The cardiac cycle

One complete beat — contraction (systole) and relaxation (diastole) of the four chambers — is the cardiac cycle. At a rate of 72–75 beats a minute it lasts 0.8 s:

Phase Duration What happens
Atrial systole 0.1 s the atria contract and top up the ventricles (about 20 % of filling)
Ventricular systole 0.3 s AV valves close (S1); pressure rises; semilunar valves open; blood is ejected
Ventricular diastole 0.5 s semilunar valves close (S2); ventricles relax and fill; AV valves open

The pressure changes drive everything:

Event Pressure relation Result
AV valves close ventricular > atrial first heart sound
Semilunar valves open ventricular > aorta / pulmonary artery ejection begins
Semilunar valves close aorta > ventricular second heart sound
AV valves open atrial > ventricular rapid filling

Typical pressures: left ventricle 120/0–10 mmHg, aorta 120/80, left atrium about 8 mmHg, right atrium about 2 mmHg.

Heart sounds. S1 ("lub") is the closure of the AV valves at the start of ventricular systole — longer and lower. S2 ("dub") is the closure of the semilunar valves at the end of systole — shorter and sharper. S3 and S4 are soft filling sounds, often inaudible in health.

Cardiac output

Stroke volume (SV) is the blood ejected by one ventricle in one beat — about 70 mL. Heart rate (HR) is the number of beats per minute — about 72. Cardiac output (CO) is the volume pumped by one ventricle in a minute:

CO = SV \times HR

CO = 70\ \text{mL} \times 72\ \text{min}^{-1} = 5040\ \text{mL min}^{-1} \approx 5\ \text{L min}^{-1}

The ejection fraction is the fraction of the end-diastolic volume that is ejected:

EF = \frac{SV}{EDV} = \frac{70}{120} \approx 0.58\ (58\ \%)

Cardiac output rises in exercise to 20–25 L min⁻¹, by increasing both rate and stroke volume. It depends on:

Factor Effect
Preload (venous return) more filling → more stretch → stronger contraction (Frank–Starling law)
Afterload (arterial pressure) higher pressure → harder to eject → lower stroke volume
Contractility adrenaline and sympathetic nerves increase it
Heart rate up to a point raises output; too fast shortens filling and lowers it

The electrocardiogram

The ECG records the electrical activity of the heart from the body surface. Its three waves:

Wave Meaning Duration
P atrial depolarisation (just before atrial systole) 0.08–0.10 s
QRS ventricular depolarisation (atrial repolarisation is hidden inside it) 0.08–0.12 s
T ventricular repolarisation —

The PR interval (0.12–0.20 s) shows the AV nodal delay; a long PR means heart block. ST elevation is the classic sign of a myocardial infarction.

Cardiac output at rest and in exercise

Problem. At rest a student has a stroke volume of 70 mL and a heart rate of 72 min⁻¹. In exercise his stroke volume rises to 120 mL and his rate to 150 min⁻¹. Find both cardiac outputs.

Solution. Rest: 70 \times 72 = 5040 mL min⁻¹ ≈ 5.0 L min⁻¹. Exercise: 120 \times 150 = 18\,000 mL min⁻¹ = 18 L min⁻¹.

So the output can rise more than threefold, and most of the rise comes from the stroke volume at first, then from the rate.

Ejection fraction

Problem. A patient's end-diastolic volume is 120 mL and end-systolic volume 50 mL. Find the stroke volume and the ejection fraction.

Solution. SV = 120 - 50 = 70 mL. EF = 70/120 = 0.58 = 58 %.

A failing heart may have an ejection fraction below 40 %, which is why it tires on exertion.

7.2 Arterial and venous systems; blood pressure

Artery, vein and capillary

Feature Artery Vein Capillary
Wall thick, three coats, much elastic and smooth muscle thin, little muscle one cell thick (endothelium + basement membrane)
Lumen narrow, stays round wide, collapses when empty extremely narrow (7–10 μm)
Valves none (except at the heart) yes, especially in the limbs none
Blood flow fast, pulsatile slow, steady slowest — the widest total cross-section
Pressure high (120/80 in the aorta) low (near 0 in the vena cava) falls from arteriole to venule
Carries blood away from the heart blood towards the heart exchange between blood and tissue
Example aorta, carotid, renal artery vena cava, jugular, saphenous in every tissue

Arteries near the heart are elastic (the aorta expands with each systole and recoils in diastole, smoothing the flow into a pulse); arteries further out are muscular and control the distribution of blood. Arterioles are the main resistance vessels and set blood pressure.

The main vessels

Region Artery Vein
Head and neck common carotid → internal and external carotid internal and external jugular
Upper limb subclavian → axillary → brachial → radial and ulnar cephalic, basilic, brachial
Thorax descending thoracic aorta azygos, hemiazygos
Abdomen coeliac trunk, superior and inferior mesenteric, renal, gonadal hepatic, renal, mesenteric
Lower limb common iliac → external iliac → femoral → popliteal great saphenous, femoral, popliteal
Whole body aorta (largest artery) vena cava (largest vein)

The aorta has three parts: ascending, the arch (giving the brachiocephalic, left common carotid and left subclavian), and the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta, which ends by dividing into the two common iliac arteries. The superior vena cava drains the head, neck and arms; the inferior vena cava drains everything below the diaphragm.

The hepatic portal system

A portal system is a set of veins that breaks into a second capillary bed before reaching the heart. The hepatic portal vein is formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric vein and the splenic vein (joined by the inferior mesenteric and gastric veins). It carries absorbed glucose, amino acids, vitamins and also drugs and toxins from the gut to the sinusoids of the liver. There the liver stores, converts or detoxifies them, and the blood leaves by the hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava.

This is why the liver is the first organ to see what we eat, and why a drug taken by mouth is partly destroyed before it reaches the rest of the body (the first-pass effect).

Blood pressure

Blood pressure is the force the blood exerts on the vessel wall. It is written as systolic/diastolic: 120/80 mmHg in a healthy young adult.

  • Systolic pressure (120) is the peak during ventricular ejection.
  • Diastolic pressure (80) is the lowest, just before the next beat.
  • Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic = 40 mmHg.
  • Mean arterial pressure ≈ diastolic + ⅓ pulse pressure ≈ 93 mmHg.

It is measured with a sphygmomanometer and a cuff on the upper arm, at the level of the heart. As the cuff deflates, the first tapping sound (Korotkoff sound) marks the systolic pressure, and the point at which the sound disappears marks the diastolic.

Category Systolic Diastolic
Hypotension below 90 below 60
Normal 90–119 60–79
Pre-hypertension / high normal 120–139 80–89
Hypertension 140 or more 90 or more
Mean arterial pressure

Problem. A patient's blood pressure is 150/95 mmHg. Find the pulse pressure and the mean arterial pressure.

Solution. Pulse pressure = 150 - 95 = 55 mmHg.

MAP = DP + \frac{PP}{3} = 95 + \frac{55}{3} = 95 + 18.3 \approx 113\ \text{mmHg}

The mean pressure is nearer the diastolic value because the heart spends about twice as long in diastole as in systole. A MAP below about 60 mmHg means the brain and kidneys are badly perfused.

Blood pressure depends on cardiac output and peripheral resistance (the radius of the arterioles), and also on blood volume, blood viscosity and the elasticity of the arteries. A vasoconstriction of the arterioles raises pressure; atherosclerosis stiffens the arteries and raises the systolic pressure.

Regulation is both nervous and hormonal:

Mechanism Where Effect
Baroreceptors carotid sinus and aortic arch stretch signals to the medulla; a rise in pressure slows the heart and dilates vessels
Chemoreceptors carotid and aortic bodies low O₂, high CO₂ → vasoconstriction and faster heart
Vasomotor centre medulla sets sympathetic tone to arterioles
Adrenaline, noradrenaline adrenal medulla, sympathetic nerves raise rate, force and resistance
Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone kidney angiotensin II constricts vessels; aldosterone retains Na⁺ and water
ADH posterior pituitary water retention, raises volume
ANP heart atria promotes Na⁺ and water loss, lowers pressure
The pulse is not the same as the heart rate in every case

The pulse is the wave felt in an artery when the aorta expands in systole. It normally equals the heart rate, but in some arrhythmias a beat is too weak to produce a wave, so the pulse rate is lower than the rate on the ECG (a pulse deficit). In an exam, "pulse rate always equals heart rate" is the wrong option.

7.3 Blood and blood groups

Blood is a fluid connective tissue: cells suspended in a liquid matrix. An adult has about 5 L (7–8 % of body mass). If a sample is spun in a centrifuge, the plasma forms about 55 % and the cells about 45 %; the percentage of cells is the haematocrit (packed cell volume).

Plasma

Plasma is 91–92 % water with 7–8 % protein and about 0.9 % inorganic salts, plus glucose, amino acids, lipids, hormones, urea and CO₂.

Protein Percentage of plasma protein Function
Albumin 55–60 % (most abundant) maintains osmotic pressure; carries fatty acids and drugs
Globulins about 35 % α and β carry lipids and vitamins; γ-globulins are antibodies
Fibrinogen about 4 % converted to fibrin in clotting

Serum is plasma without fibrinogen — that is, the fluid left after blood has clotted.

The formed elements

Cell Count per mm³ Structure Function Life span
Red blood cells (erythrocytes) 4.5–5.5 million biconcave disc, no nucleus in man, filled with haemoglobin carry O₂ and CO₂ 120 days
Neutrophils 3000–6000 (60–70 % of WBC) lobed nucleus, granular phagocytosis of bacteria — the first responders hours to days
Eosinophils 2–4 % bilobed, red granules attack parasites; allergy days
Basophils 0.5–1 % lobed, blue granules release histamine and heparin days
Lymphocytes 20–30 % round nucleus, little cytoplasm B cells make antibodies; T cells kill infected cells years
Monocytes 2–8 % kidney-shaped nucleus, largest WBC become macrophages months
Platelets (thrombocytes) 1.5–4 lakh cell fragments from megakaryocytes haemostasis 8–10 days

Erythropoiesis — the making of red cells — happens in the red bone marrow of ribs, sternum, vertebrae and pelvis, under the hormone erythropoietin from the kidney, which rises when the kidney senses low oxygen. It needs iron (for haem), vitamin B₁₂ and folic acid (for DNA in dividing cells) and vitamin B₆. Old red cells are destroyed by macrophages in the spleen, liver and bone marrow; the iron is recycled and the haem is converted to bilirubin.

Haemostasis — stopping bleeding

  1. Vascular spasm — the cut vessel constricts.
  2. Platelet plug — platelets stick to the collagen, swell and aggregate.
  3. Coagulation — the clotting cascade. Tissue damage exposes thromboplastin (factor III), which with Ca²⁺ and other factors converts prothrombin (II) → thrombin. Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen (I) into insoluble fibrin threads that trap the cells into a clot.
  4. Clot retraction and repair — the clot shrinks, and fibroblasts repair the vessel.
  5. Fibrinolysis — plasmin dissolves the clot once the vessel is healed.

There are 13 clotting factors. Vitamin K is needed by the liver to make prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X, and Ca²⁺ (factor IV) is required at several steps — which is why calcium-binding drugs such as citrate stop blood clotting in a bottle. Heparin, from basophils and mast cells, is a natural anticoagulant.

Blood groups — ABO and Rh

Karl Landsteiner described the ABO groups in 1900. The red cell carries agglutinogens (antigens) and the plasma carries agglutinins (antibodies) against the antigens it does not have:

Group Agglutinogen on RBC Agglutinin in plasma Can receive red cells from
A A anti-B A, O
B B anti-A B, O
AB A and B none A, B, AB, O
O none anti-A and anti-B O only

A transfusion of the wrong group makes the donor cells clump (agglutination) and then burst (haemolysis), releasing haemoglobin that can block the kidney tubules — a transfusion reaction.

  • O negative is the universal donor of red cells: its cells carry no A, B or D antigen, so no recipient's antibodies can attack them.
  • AB positive is the universal recipient: its plasma has no anti-A, anti-B or anti-D.

The Rh factor (rhesus antigen, D antigen) was found by Landsteiner and Wiener in 1940. About 85 % of people are Rh positive. Anti-D is not present naturally; it appears only after an Rh-negative person is exposed to Rh- positive blood.

Erythroblastosis fetalis (haemolytic disease of the newborn). An Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus is sensitised at delivery, when fetal cells enter her blood, and makes anti-D IgG. In a later pregnancy with another Rh-positive fetus, that IgG crosses the placenta and destroys the fetal red cells: the baby is born anaemic and jaundiced, and may die. It is prevented by giving the mother anti-D immunoglobulin after the first delivery.

The donor rule is about red cells, not plasma

"O negative is the universal donor" is true for packed red cells. If whole plasma were transfused, O plasma contains anti-A and anti-B and would attack A or B recipient cells. The paper asks the red-cell rule; answer O negative, but know why.

7.4 Cardiovascular disorders

Disorder What happens Cause / risk Key feature
Atherosclerosis fatty streaks → plaque of cholesterol, cells and calcium in the arterial intima; lumen narrows and the wall stiffens high LDL, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, family history angina, heart attack, stroke, gangrene
Angina pectoris reversible ischaemia of the heart muscle narrowed coronary arteries crushing chest pain on exertion, relieved by rest or nitrates
Myocardial infarction (heart attack) a coronary artery is blocked by a thrombus; part of the muscle dies plaque rupture, smoking, hypertension severe chest pain radiating to the left arm and jaw, sweating, ST elevation, troponin rises
Hypertension sustained BP ≥ 140/90 age, salt, obesity, stress, kidney disease "silent killer": stroke, heart failure, kidney damage
Varicose veins dilated, tortuous, elongated veins with incompetent valves long standing, pregnancy, heredity aching legs, visible blue swellings; worse in the lower limb
Anaemia haemoglobin below normal iron deficiency (commonest), B₁₂ deficiency, blood loss, haemolysis pallor, fatigue, breathlessness, fast pulse
Stroke blood supply to part of the brain is cut thrombus, embolus, haemorrhage sudden weakness, speech loss

Atherosclerosis begins with injury to the endothelium; LDL cholesterol enters the wall, is oxidised, and macrophages swallow it to become "foam cells". Smooth muscle and collagen form a fibrous cap over a lipid core. A plaque may rupture, exposing the core to blood, and a clot forms on it — the event that causes most heart attacks and strokes.

Anaemia is classified by the size of the red cells:

Type Cause Cell size
Iron-deficiency poor diet, blood loss, pregnancy microcytic, hypochromic
Pernicious lack of intrinsic factor → no B₁₂ absorption macrocytic
Haemolytic red cells destroyed (malaria, sickle cell, Rh disease) normal or abnormal shape
Aplastic bone marrow fails (drugs, radiation) few cells of all types
Telling the chest pains apart

Angina: pain on exertion, lasts minutes, relieved by rest or a nitrate, no enzyme rise. Heart attack: pain at rest, lasts longer, not relieved, with sweating and nausea, ECG changes and raised troponin. That single contrast answers most clinical stems.

Formula and fact sheet

The heart

ECG

Vessels and pressure

Fact Value

Hypertension ≥ 140/90
Hypotension < 90/60

Portal vein formed by superior mesenteric + splenic veins

Blood

Fact Value

Blood groups

Group Antigen Antibody
A A anti-B
B B anti-A

  • Universal donor (red cells): O negative.
  • Universal recipient: AB positive.
  • Rh positive: about 85 %; anti-D causes erythroblastosis fetalis.
  • ABO described by Landsteiner (1900); Rh by Landsteiner and Wiener (1940).

Traps

  1. The left ventricle wall is thickest.
  2. The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood; the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.
  3. O negative is the universal donor; AB positive the universal recipient.
  4. S1 = AV valves, S2 = semilunar valves.
  5. Most CO₂ is carried as bicarbonate (unit 6), not by red cells alone.
  6. Veins have valves; arteries do not.
  7. The SA node, not the AV node, is the pacemaker.
  8. Cardiac output = SV × HR, not SV + HR.

Chapter summary

  • The heart (250–300 g) lies in the mediastinum inside the pericardium; its wall is epicardium, myocardium (thickest in the left ventricle) and endocardium.
  • Four chambers and four valves: tricuspid and bicuspid (mitral) AV valves with chordae tendineae, and the pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves; all open and close passively.
  • Double circulation: right ventricle → lungs → left atrium (pulmonary); left ventricle → body → right atrium (systemic). The coronary arteries arise from the ascending aorta.
  • The SA node (70–80 min⁻¹) is the pacemaker because it depolarises fastest; the impulse passes SA → AV → bundle of His → Purkinje, with a 0.1 s delay at the AV node.
  • The cardiac cycle lasts 0.8 s: atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, diastole 0.5 s; S1 is AV valve closure, S2 semilunar closure.
  • CO = SV × HR ≈ 70 × 72 ≈ 5 L min⁻¹; ejection fraction ≈ 60 %; exercise raises output to 20–25 L min⁻¹.
  • ECG: P = atrial depolarisation, QRS = ventricular depolarisation, T = ventricular repolarisation.
  • Arteries are thick-walled, valveless and high-pressure; veins are thin-walled, valved and low-pressure; the hepatic portal vein carries gut blood to the liver before the heart.
  • BP 120/80; hypertension ≥ 140/90; baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch; the medulla sets vasomotor tone.
  • Blood is 55 % plasma and 45 % cells; RBC 5 million/mm³ and 120 days, WBC 4000–11 000/mm³, platelets 1.5–4 lakh/mm³; albumin is the commonest plasma protein.
  • Haemostasis: spasm → platelet plug → prothrombin → thrombin → fibrin → clot retraction → fibrinolysis.
  • ABO: A has anti-B, B has anti-A, AB has none, O has both; O− donor, AB+ recipient; Rh incompatibility causes erythroblastosis fetalis.
  • Disorders: atherosclerosis (plaque), angina (reversible), MI (thrombus, troponin), varicose veins (valve failure), anaemia (low haemoglobin).

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (c) — the SA node, in the wall of the right atrium, depolarises fastest and so sets the rhythm.

2. (b) — the bicuspid or mitral valve, on the left side; the tricuspid is on the right.

3. (d) — two atria and two ventricles, making the heart a double pump.

4. (a) — the pericardium, with fibrous and serous layers and a film of fluid between them.

5. (b) — 0.8 s, made up of atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s and diastole 0.5 s.

6. (a) — about 70 mL per beat; 120 mL is the end-diastolic volume and 50 mL the end-systolic volume.

7. (c) — 70 mL × 72 ≈ 5 L per minute.

8. (d) — S1 is the closure of the AV valves at the start of ventricular systole; S2 is the closure of the semilunar valves.
